title: From the Roof Down
logline: A large disused tiled and timber-framed building in a hill valley is not demolished but taken apart in the reverse of the order it was built in — ridge tiles, tiles counted off in fours, battens, rafters, king posts, wall plates, door and window frames knocked out whole — until nothing is left but a floor with the plan of its rooms still drawn on it, and every piece of it is standing numbered in a yard waiting to be part of something else.
human_question: If everything a thing was made of can be released without being broken, what exactly is left when it is gone?

place.what_kind_of_place: A hill valley in the middle of the island, a long flat basin between two ranges, with the older building stock of a colonial-era district town and its villages still standing in it: hipped roofs of flat clay tiles laid in courses, timber frames of jak and satin and nadun cut when those trees were near at hand, lime-plastered rubble walls a foot and a half thick, doors and windows framed as complete units that were built into the wall rather than fitted afterwards, and floors of cement or of red-polished screed. In among them, in a compound off a road, one such building that has been out of use for years: a long single-storey store with a hipped roof, an open floor divided by low partitions, and a roof space that has had nobody in it for a decade. The working equipment is small and almost entirely hand tools: crowbars, claw hammers, a hand saw, wooden wedges, coir and nylon rope, a plank ramp, a wheelbarrow, chalk, a tape, a ladder, and stacks of empty gunnies for the tiles. A few kilometres away, on the road, the other half of the place: a yard of reclaimed materials, with tiles stacked in fours under tin, rafters and wall plates stickered in tiers, door and window frames leaning in rows like a gate they will never be in, and a man with a ledger who knows which building each row came out of.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the sequence is fixed, visible from the air, and runs one way. From height at the start, the building reads as a single solid object: a ridge, four hips, several thousand tiles in courses, and a shadow. From height at the end, the same frame holds a clean rectangle of floor, open to the sky, with the plan of every room still drawn across it in plaster lines and old paint, and the trees around it standing exactly where they were. Between those two frames nothing has been broken, nothing has been burnt and nothing has been thrown away. Close, the work is a long series of small, precise, reversible acts: a ridge tile lifted with two fingers under it; tiles counted off in fours and passed hand to hand down a ladder; battens levered up and the nails drawn and kept; rafters lowered on a rope one at a time; a king post taken out and chalked with the name of the building; a door frame worked loose from the masonry with wedges and lifted out whole, still square. And one moment that will only happen once: the first daylight reaching a floor that has been under a roof since the day it was laid.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Everything, in strict reverse order, without any of it being destroyed. The building can only be undone in the order it was made, from the top down, and no step can be skipped: nothing under a tile can be reached while the tile is on. Once a course is off it does not go back on. The number of things in the building falls all day while the number of things in the yard rises, and the total does not change. Across a longer clock the parts keep moving: tiles off this roof will be sorted, and the sound ones will be on another roof inside a year; a rafter may be in its third building; the yard has rows in it whose original buildings no longer exist anywhere. And the ground the building stood on is not scraped, filled or cleared: the floor stays, with its plan on it, and the weather starts on it.
place.when_it_looks_best: A dry spell, because the roof comes off first and everything under it is exposed from that hour on, and because tiles are not handled on wet ladders. Within the day, the roof wants the first two hours, when low sun runs along the courses and every tile has an edge; the moment daylight first reaches the floor wants whatever hour it happens in and cannot be given to the light; and the bare floor wants noon from directly overhead, because that is the only time the plan of the rooms reads as a drawing rather than as a ruin. The yard wants the last hour, when the stacks separate from one another. The one shot that has to be planned for in advance is the aerial of the whole roof before anything is touched, because after the first morning it does not exist.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about a building being taken to pieces instead of knocked down. A hipped roof from the air with several thousand tiles in courses; a ridge tile lifted with two fingers; tiles counted off in fours and passed hand to hand down a ladder into gunnies; nails drawn from battens and dropped into a tin; rafters lowered one at a time on a rope; a king post chalked; a door frame wedged out of a wall and lifted away whole and still square; and then a floor open to the sky with the plan of its rooms drawn on it. Then a yard on a road where all of it is standing in rows, stickered and numbered, and a ledger that knows which building each row came out of. It has a complete shape with nothing said over it, and anyone who likes old carpentry, careful work, or the fact that a house is a kit that can be taken back to its parts, has a whole piece here.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same fortnight becomes the fourth and last of the ultimate realities the series has been working through since its first film, and the film's whole discipline is not to pretend it can show it. The sources describe that reality as the only one not produced by any condition: it does not arise, change or pass, it has no shape, place or content, it is not a pleasant feeling, and it is nonetheless real and not an empty nothing. They say it is not built by effort at all but uncovered, that it is very near and simply covered over, and that describing it to somebody who has not seen it is like describing a colour to somebody born blind. A building coming off its own floor from the top down is the nearest thing a camera can be honest about: an uncovering, done carefully, in which nothing is made and nothing is destroyed. So the voice uses it as a picture and then says, twice and in plain words, that the picture is not the thing, that the empty floor is not the thing, that a long quiet is not the thing either, and that there is no shot of it in this film or in any other.

sequence.on_screen: First light, high and square over the building before anything has been touched. A ridge, four hips, several thousand flat tiles in courses, a shadow across the compound, trees around it, a road. It reads as one solid object.
sequence.voice: The last of the four basic realities this series began with is the only one in the list that nothing produces. It does not arise, it does not change, it does not pass; it has no shape, no place and no content; it is not a feeling; and both sources insist that it is real all the same and not an empty nothing [C073-P:L18–L20; C073-P:L52–L58]. It cannot be filmed. This film is not going to pretend otherwise, and it will say so more than once.

sequence.on_screen: Before a tile is lifted. A tape run along the roof and a number written down. Tiles counted by the course. Door and window frames measured and listed with chalk on the plaster beside them. A man on a ladder looking into the roof space with a torch, and whatever is living in it. The last few things in the building carried out and put in a van.
sequence.voice: The texts attach four ordinary duties to the deepest withdrawal they describe: make safe the things you will not be able to reach, stay answerable to your community, stay answerable to your teacher, and know honestly how much time you have [C102-P:L43–L62]. Here the same list runs the other way round. Nothing is being kept back for a return, so everything that cannot look after itself has to be somewhere else before the covering comes off — and the sources restrict what they are describing to rare people who are already free, which nobody on this roof is [C102-P:L31].

sequence.on_screen: The roof coming off. A ridge tile lifted with two fingers under it. Tiles counted off in fours and passed hand to hand down a ladder into gunnies. Battens levered up, nails drawn and dropped into a tin. Then the first daylight falling onto a floor that has been in shade since the day it was laid, and dust standing in it.
sequence.voice: The sources are firm on one point that is easy to get wrong. This peace is not manufactured: it is realised, not produced [C073-P:L20]. The Margaya puts it plainly — it is very near, and simply covered over, and what effort does is clear the covering rather than make anything [C073-M:L13–L15]. So this is what an uncovering looks like when somebody does it carefully. It is not what the sources are talking about.

sequence.on_screen: The timber. Rafters lowered one at a time on a rope. A king post taken out and chalked with the name of the building. A wall plate off. Then the yard a few kilometres away: rafters stickered in tiers, tiles in fours under tin, frames leaning in rows, a ledger open. Then a roof somewhere nearby with rafters in it that came out of a building that no longer exists.
sequence.voice: When the Pradeepika has to say how something can be real without having a place of its own, it uses fire. Fire appears wherever its conditions are brought together, it has no fixed home, and however many lamps are burning nobody calls them different fires [C073-P:L64–L68]. The sources say the same of this: there is one of it, however many people come to it [C073-P:L68; C073-M:L31]. None of that is a claim about these beams. The beams are timber, and they are going into other people's roofs.

sequence.on_screen: The bare rectangle. Walls down to knee height. Doorways with no doors in them. The floor open to the sky with the plan of the rooms drawn across it in plaster lines and old paint. A gap in the trees where the ridge used to be. Nothing at all happening.
sequence.voice: And a guard the group needs here, because an empty floor is very easy to mistake for an answer. The sources describe existences far longer and far quieter than anything a person can imagine: mind without any body at all, lasting tens of thousands of great aeons [C015-P:L23–L30]. And they still count those among the ordinary, worldly minds and not among the goal, because however refined and however long, a result is a thing that ends [C015-M:L22; C015-P:L41]. A long quiet is not it. Having little is not it. This floor is not it.

sequence.on_screen: Noon, from directly overhead, held very long and without a cut. The floor, the plan, the shadow of nothing. Then the same frame at ground level, with a hand not quite touching a plaster line.
sequence.voice: Both sources admit how hard this is to talk about. The Pradeepika says that explaining it to somebody who has not seen it is like explaining a colour to somebody born blind: you can be told about it by others, and you can reason your way towards it, and the reasoning gives you an inference and nothing better [C073-P:L104–L108]. So this is the film's position, stated plainly. What is in this frame is a clean floor with the drawing of a house on it, and it is beautiful, and it is not the thing. There is no shot of the thing.

sequence.on_screen: Last light in the yard. Tiles in fours, rafters stickered, frames leaning in rows, the ledger closed, a lorry loaded and going out of the gate. Then the floor again, small in the frame, with the first rain of the evening on it.
sequence.voice: What the sources will say about the good they are pointing at is that it is a freedom from something rather than a pleasure in something: a release, and not a feeling that anybody could have [C073-P:L18; C073-M:L5–L7]. What a building taken down like this can show is only this much. That a thing can be emptied and released without being broken. That nothing new was made when the covering came off. And that everything that was in it is now somewhere else, holding somebody else's roof up.

concept_merge.why_together: C073 is the group's final concept and the whole subject of the film, and the film's work is to carry it without faking it. The digest gives it as the fourth ultimate reality, unproduced by any condition, without arising, ageing or passing, without material or mental content, not a place and not a pleasant feeling, and real rather than an empty nothing [C073-P:L18–L20; C073-P:L52–L58]; as realised rather than manufactured [C073-P:L20]; as very near and simply covered over, with effort clearing the covering [C073-M:L13–L15]; as real without a location, argued through the simile of fire appearing wherever its conditions come together [C073-P:L64–L68]; as one, however many realise it [C073-P:L68; C073-M:L31]; as beyond the reach of reasoning, with the colour-and-blindness comparison [C073-P:L104–L108]; and as a release rather than a felt pleasure [C073-P:L18; C073-M:L5–L7]. C015 supplies the guard the ending needs, because the film's most beautiful frame is an empty floor and an empty floor is exactly what a viewer will mistake for the answer: the sources' longest and most refined existences, mind without body for tens of thousands of aeons, are still counted among the eighty-one worldly minds and are still results that end [C015-P:L23–L30; C015-M:L22; C015-P:L41]. C102 supplies the shape of a responsible release, the four preliminary duties run backwards: everything that cannot look after itself is found somewhere else before the covering comes off, and nothing is kept for a return [C102-P:L43–L62], with the digest's restriction of the attainment itself to rare, already-liberated people spoken in the same breath so that no equivalence is drawn [C102-P:L31]. A building taken apart in the reverse of the order it was built in is the one process available to a camera in which something is completely emptied and completely released while nothing in it is destroyed.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the group's last claim is a negative one, and that the honest way to film a negative claim is to film something that looks like it and then say, on screen, that it is not it. Uncovering rather than building is the source's own distinction, and a roof coming off a floor from the top down is the only literal uncovering available: nothing under a tile can be reached until the tile is off, nothing is made when the light gets in, and the space that was inside is the same space that is now outside. The film gets three of the digest's hardest statements for nothing, because the material states them: that the thing is not produced, that describing it is like describing a colour to somebody who cannot see, and that it is a release rather than a pleasure. And it gets its own correction in the same fortnight, because the emptied floor is immediately followed by the reminder that the longest and quietest result in the sources is still only a result. This idea has been round once before. Its first version filmed an elderly householder giving away a home of sixty years: that is dropped because it made a named person's old age and dispossession the exhibit, because it risked reading a reduced life as an attainment, and because no real person should be placed where this concept sits. The subject has moved to a building that belongs to no household, with no person's ageing anywhere in it, and the concept is unchanged.

concept_links.why: The film is the digest's account of the fourth reality and its own admissions of difficulty, and nothing else. The opening beat states the negations — unproduced, not arising, not ageing, not passing, no shape, no place, no content, not a feeling, and not an empty nothing [C073-P:L18–L20; C073-P:L52–L58] — and says in the same breath that it cannot be filmed. The distinction between realising and producing is spoken over the roof coming off [C073-P:L20], with the Margaya's 'very near and simply covered' beside it [C073-M:L13–L15]. The fire simile is spoken as the source's own way of talking about something real without a location, and the voice immediately says it is not a claim about the timber [C073-P:L64–L68], and the oneness of it is given with it [C073-P:L68; C073-M:L31]. The colour-and-blindness comparison and the limit of reasoning are spoken over the film's single most beautiful shot, precisely so that the shot cannot be read as the thing [C073-P:L104–L108]. The closing beat gives release rather than felt pleasure [C073-P:L18; C073-M:L5–L7]. Every limit in the digest is honoured and most of them are on screen. It is not filmed as inner peace, calm or relaxation: nobody is still, nobody meditates, and no mood is offered. It is not filmed as a place or a destination: the film's empty floor is named as a floor. It is not filmed as nothingness or annihilation: the whole point of the subject is that nothing is destroyed and every part goes on being used. It is not presented as produced, achieved or created, and nobody in the film is doing anything spiritual. It is not made personal: the source's one-of-it is spoken. The stages, the with-and-without-residue pair and the three names are all left out, because none of them could sit over any footage without faking, and the Margaya's pawning argument is not used because there is no household finance in this film. Nibbāna is not filmed, and the voice says twice that there is no shot of it.

This link exists for one beat and one purpose: to stop the emptied floor from reading as the answer. The digest's warning is exact — a formless existence, however long and however refined, is still a result that ends, and the sources count these minds among the eighty-one worldly ones rather than the supramundane [C015-M:L22; C015-P:L41] — and the film speaks it over the bare rectangle, together with the source's own measure of that duration [C015-P:L23–L30]. The digest's limits are honoured. The cake-and-rice image is flagged in the digest as a teaching illustration that should not be quoted as a canonical claim, and it is not used. The remark about a happiness close to the final one is not used either. 'Actions without consequences' is not turned into a slogan, and the functional minds are not attributed to anybody: nobody in the film is described as free, as beyond result, or as having any attainment [C015-P:L39; C015-M:L14]. The fast-and-slow learner distinction is not used at all, and nobody's capability is ranked. Nothing in the film presents living with little, living quietly or living alone as a stage on any road, and no person's circumstances are read as a spiritual condition.

C102 gives the release its shape and keeps it from looking like abandonment. The four preliminary duties tie even the deepest withdrawal to the safety of what is left behind, to the community, to a teacher and to the time one has [C102-P:L43–L62]; the film speaks them over the counting, listing and clearing that happen before a single tile is lifted, and states that here the list runs the other way, because nothing is being held for a return. The digest's restriction is spoken in the same beat: what the sources describe is available only to rare people who are already free, so no equivalence is drawn with anybody on the roof [C102-P:L31]. Every limit in the digest that bears on this film is honoured. Cessation is not presented as switching off, a rest or a detox, and nothing in the film is presented as an entry into anything. It is not offered as an escape from responsibility — the whole beat is about responsibilities discharged before the covering comes off. It is not linked to death, to coma or to anything medical, and the building's ending is never allowed to stand for a person's. The phrase about dwelling at ease here and now is deliberately not spoken, because there is nothing on screen it could honestly sit over, and the seven-day limit is not used.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the last of the four realities this series has been working through is the one thing in the list that nothing produces: it does not arise, change or pass, it has no place, shape or content, it is not a pleasant feeling, and the sources still insist it is real and not an empty nothing. That they describe it as uncovered rather than built, and as very near and simply covered over. That they are open about how hard it is to speak of, comparing the attempt to describing a colour to someone born blind, and that reasoning about it yields inference only. And that neither a cleared space, nor a long quiet, nor having very little is the thing, because even the longest and most refined existence in these texts is still a result that ends. The building is an image of uncovering and the film says so twice; there is no shot of the unconditioned anywhere in it.
what_must_be_real: A building that was coming down anyway, taken apart in the order and at the speed the gang would take it apart, with the owner's permission and the gang's. No course of tiles is put back so that it can be lifted again on better light; no frame is re-set in a wall; no rafter is re-hung; nothing is pre-loosened before a shot, and no part of the sequence is reordered to suit the camera. The one unrepeatable moment in the film — the first daylight reaching the floor — is filmed in whatever light it happens in or not at all. Nothing is broken, burnt or thrown away for effect, and if parts of the building are in fact rotten, worthless or unsalvageable, the film shows that rather than implying that everything can be saved. No plaster line, mark, painted name or notice on the walls is added, cleaned or arranged, and anything that identifies a former occupant is kept off screen. Whatever is living in the roof space is dealt with the way the gang deals with it, and nothing is disturbed for a shot. Nobody is named or followed as a character; nobody's care, patience or skill is presented as an attainment; nobody is asked to confirm, illustrate or comment on any doctrine; and nobody is asked whether the building means anything to them. The ground the building stood on is not cleaned, swept, dressed or lit for the final frames.
position_hint: last in the group, and the group's own ending rather than the series': it is where the fourth reality has to be spoken, and it is built so that the speaking is mostly denial. It has to come after the film about withdrawal, because the responsible-release beat depends on the viewer having already watched the four duties run forwards, and it has to come before the group's closing film, which lets ordinary conditions resume after it. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Faking the unconditioned. A clean floor open to the sky at noon is the most seductive image in the whole group, and if the voice does not say plainly that it is not the thing, the film has lied about the one subject it exists to be honest about.
Letting the fire simile slide into a claim that the timber, the light or the space is the thing, when the source uses it only to say that something can be real without having a place.
Letting the emptying read as an achievement or a release earned by anybody, or the gang's care read as reverence.
Letting a building's ending stand in for a person's death, which the group's floor forbids outright and which an empty room invites.
Reading a cleared, quiet, minimal space as the answer, which is exactly what the second concept is in the film to prevent.
Aestheticising demolition, so that the pleasure is loss rather than release, or making the building's disuse a lament for a vanished way of building.
Turning the reclaimed-materials trade into a message about sustainability, which would replace the concept with a cause.
Exposing a former occupant or owner through a painted name, a notice, a letterhead or a mark left on a wall.
Romanticising the work. Stripping a roof from a ladder with several thousand tiles to move is how people fall, and nothing about how any of it is handled may be arranged for a shot.
drop_if: No building of this kind is being taken apart for its materials inside the window, so the sequence would have to be staged on a building that was going to be knocked down.
The owner or the gang will not allow the whole sequence to be followed on their own terms, in their own order, from the untouched roof to the bare floor.
The work is done with a machine, so that the building is broken rather than released and the film's central fact is gone.
The bare floor is cleared, filled or built over immediately, so the film's last frames do not exist.
Height cannot be obtained over the compound, so the two frames the film is built on — the whole roof and the bare plan — cannot be made.
A former occupant's name or details cannot be kept off screen while the walls are filmed.

connections.note: From securing a place you intend to come back to, to releasing one with nothing kept back and no return arranged.
This one empties something and says plainly that the emptiness is not the answer; the next lets ordinary conditions start up again afterwards.

selection.reason: It is the only process available to a camera in which something is completely emptied and completely released while nothing in it is destroyed, and it is built so that the group's unfilmable concept is named as unfilmable twice on screen.

review.note: Rewritten and relocated 2026-09-24. The previous version filmed an elderly householder giving away a home of sixty years; that is dropped because it made a named person's old age and dispossession the exhibit, because a reduced life would inevitably have read as an attainment, and because this is the concept beside which no real person should be placed. The concepts are unchanged and all three links are kept, re-grounded and rewritten. The subject is now a disused tiled and timber-framed building taken apart in the reverse of the order it was built in, so that it is emptied and released without any of it being destroyed, with no household, no home and nobody's ageing anywhere in the film. Because this idea carries C073, the file was written on the assumption that the unfilmable would be faked if it were not guarded explicitly: the first beat says the thing cannot be filmed, the sixth beat says over the film's most beautiful shot that the shot is not the thing and that there is no shot of the thing, the fire simile is immediately disclaimed as not being a statement about the timber, and C015 is used for one beat only, to say that an emptied floor, a long quiet and having little are none of them the answer. C073's five stages, its with-residue and without-residue pair, its three names and the Margaya's pawning argument are all deliberately unused, because none of them could be attached to footage without faking. C015's cake-and-rice image and its remark about a happiness close to the final one are flagged in that digest as needing a teacher's framing and are not used. C102's phrase about dwelling at ease here and now is left unspoken for the same reason it is left unspoken in the previous film. Every citation was re-tested against its digest's own evidence before use, including the ranges most likely to be got wrong by one line: C073-P:L18–L20, C073-P:L52–L58, C073-P:L64–L68, C073-P:L104–L108, C073-M:L13–L15, C073-M:L5–L7, C015-P:L23–L30 and C102-P:L43–L62 are all ranges the digests themselves cite.

suggested_location.name: The old tiled and timber-framed building stock of the Matale valley, and the reclaimed-materials yards on its roads

also_known_as.name: kaballa
also_known_as.meaning: the flat clay roof tile that these roofs are laid in, counted, carried and stacked in fours; the older hand-made ones are the part of a building most sought after when it comes down

also_known_as.name: palu lee
also_known_as.meaning: loosely, old timber: second-hand structural timber from a building that has been taken down, sold on for reuse rather than as firewood. Reported as ordinary trade speech and not confirmed with anybody in the trade

also_known_as.name: walauwa
also_known_as.meaning: a large old house of the kind that supplies much of this material when one is taken down; used here only as the building type, since the film's subject is deliberately not a dwelling

suggested_location.region: Matale District, Central Province: the long flat valley between two ranges in the centre of the island, with its colonial-era district town, its village roads and the older building stock standing along them
suggested_location.why_here: Because the material the film needs is standing here in quantity and is steadily coming down. This is a valley whose building stock was largely put up between the middle of the nineteenth century and the middle of the twentieth, in the district's plantation and administrative period, and the way it was built is exactly what makes it takeable apart: hipped roofs of flat clay tiles laid loose in courses on battens, frames of hardwood cut locally when those trees were near at hand, door and window frames made as complete units and built into the wall rather than fitted into a hole in it, and thick lime-plastered rubble walls. A roof like that can be undone tile by tile without breaking anything, and a frame like that can be wedged out of a wall and stood up somewhere else still square. The district also sits in the middle of the island, on the main roads to three provinces, which is why reclaimed tile and timber has somewhere to go from here. That gives the film both halves of its subject within a few kilometres: one building coming down in a compound, and a yard on a road where its parts stand numbered in rows beside rows from buildings that no longer exist. And crucially the subject can be found in a form that is not anybody's home: disused stores, works buildings and outbuildings of this period are common here, they belong to companies and public bodies rather than to households, and no person's age, loss or dispossession is anywhere in the film.
what_to_film: The whole roof from height, square on, in the first two hours, before anything is touched — the single shot that cannot be made again after the first morning.
The counting and listing before any work: the tape along the roof, tiles counted by the course, frames measured and chalked, the last things carried out of the building.
A torch into the roof space, and whatever is living there, filmed as the gang finds it and without disturbing it.
The first ridge tile lifted with two fingers under it, close and slow.
Tiles counted off in fours and passed hand to hand down a ladder into gunnies, held long enough that the rhythm and the count are clear.
Battens levered up and nails drawn and dropped into a tin, at arm's length.
The first daylight reaching the floor, in whatever light it happens in.
Rafters lowered one at a time on a rope, a king post taken out and chalked, a wall plate coming off.
A door or window frame worked out of masonry with wedges and lifted away whole and still square.
The bare floor from directly overhead at noon, held very long without a cut, with the plan of the rooms reading as a drawing.
The yard: tiles in fours under tin, rafters stickered in tiers, frames leaning in rows, the ledger open on a table.
A roof somewhere nearby with reclaimed timber in it, filmed plainly, so that the parts are seen in use rather than only in stock.
The floor again at the end, small in frame, with the first weather on it.
suggested_location.access: By road from the hill capital or from the north, and then on village roads and into a private compound. Everything depends on two agreements: the owner of the building, which for the film's purposes should be a company or a public body rather than a household, and the salvage contractor whose job it is, who has to be willing to be followed rather than to give a demonstration. Neither should be approached cold; the reclaimed-materials yards are the obvious way in, because they know which buildings are coming down and when. If the building is anywhere near a protected monument or is itself of a listed period, the antiquities authority has an interest and has to be asked, and a building that is protected cannot be the subject at all. The hazards are ordinary and serious: ladders, several thousand tiles to be moved by hand, rafters under load, old nails, lime dust, and a roof space nobody has been into for years. A crew has to be able to work from fixed positions outside the drop for a fortnight without asking anybody to move. Drone flight over a private compound needs the owner's agreement whatever the general rules allow, and the compound is likely to be close enough to houses that low flying is not appropriate.
suggested_location.best_time: A dry spell, and a fortnight rather than a day, taken against the contractor's own programme so that the film gets a building that is genuinely coming apart. The untouched roof has to be filmed on the first morning before work starts, which means arriving a day early. The bare floor has to be filmed at noon and then again at the end, before anything is done with the ground. One further visit to the yard, weeks later, is worth planning for, to film parts of this building standing in rows with parts of others.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, and unverified on the ground. From the sources above: the district is the centremost in the island, covers about 1,993 square kilometres, has its administrative capital and largest town in the valley, and holds a building stock substantially of the colonial and early post-colonial period; timber buildings in the country have been documented as a category in their own right; reclaimed timber from earlier structures is described as a sought-after material in present-day building here; and the practice the film depends on is attested at least once in a well-known case, in which a large house was dismantled working from the roof down, with everything salvageable including doors and windows boxed, carted away and re-erected on another site. The coordinates are a point in the valley beside the district's main town, taken from published positions of landmarks there, and are a direction towards the kind of ground the film needs rather than a survey. Almost everything specific in this record is an inference and should be treated as the first thing to check. No building has been identified, no salvage contractor or reclaimed-materials yard has been found or approached, no owner has been asked, and no permission of any kind has been sought. Four things the film depends on are unconfirmed for this district: that buildings of this type are currently being taken apart for their materials here rather than knocked down with a machine, that a disused non-domestic building of the right size is available inside a filming window, that a yard exists within a few kilometres that takes and re-sells the parts and keeps a record of where they came from, and that height can be obtained over a private compound at all. The trade speech recorded above under the local names is reported and not confirmed. No photograph of a building of this kind coming down, of a salvage gang or of a reclaimed-materials yard in this district was found on Wikimedia Commons; the one image is a general view of the valley.

unknowns: Whether buildings of this type are currently taken apart by hand for their materials in this district, or whether the work has gone over to machines that break rather than release them.
Whether a disused, non-domestic building of the right size and period is coming down inside a filming window, so that no household's home is the subject.
Whether a reclaimed-materials yard nearby takes the parts, re-sells them and keeps any record of which building each row came out of, which the film's second half depends on.
Whether the owner and the contractor will allow the whole sequence to be followed from an untouched roof to a bare floor, in their own order, over a fortnight.
Whether the bare floor survives long enough to be filmed twice, or is cleared and built over immediately.
Whether the building or its compound falls under any heritage protection that would forbid, or ought to forbid, its dismantling being filmed.
Whether height can be obtained over the compound, and whether the plan of the rooms reads from directly overhead as strongly as it appears to from the ground.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
